rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding verses prepare Moses mentally and emotionally for his mission; the following material gives signs essential for confronting Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: The previous verses guide Moses (sws) regarding the mental and emotional preparation for the mission at hand.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The staff is the most important sign and the source from which the remaining signs emanated.
rows.anchor: The most important of these signs was that of the staff from which the rest of the signs emanated.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ flight highlights how initially unfamiliar and strange prophetic experiences frighten a prophet, whom God gradually familiarizes with them.
rows.anchor: when it started to swivel like a snake, he got so frightened that he ran away without even looking back.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophethood is bestowed unexpectedly, not won by desire or demand; prophets accept its obligatory responsibility anxiously after becoming convinced of their divine appointment.
rows.anchor: their desire or demand. In fact, it is bestowed upon them without their expectation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God reassures Moses that he is safe in divine company, while those who reject the messengers face danger.
rows.anchor: in the company of God, His messengers have nothing to fear; they are absolutely safe and secure

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses is God’s messenger and his staff is a sword, so his enemies should fear him rather than he fear them.
rows.anchor: So, why should he fear them; it is they who should fear him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The righteous read trials as possible punishment for an error; Moses may have recalled killing the Copt, though he had repented and God accepted his repentance, reflecting their strong self-accountability.
rows.anchor: thought of his killing of the Copt. Even though after that he had repented and God had also accepted his repentance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God promises forgiveness to any servant who errs, then repents and atones; the generalized assurance benefits all people, not Moses alone.
rows.anchor: the benefit of the statement has encompassed all people and not just Moses (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The qualification that Moses’ hand would be white without illness dispels his doubt.
rows.anchor: “without any ailment” are meant to dispel any doubt in the mind of Moses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assurance was given as the miracle was bestowed; otherwise the fear Moses felt over the staff could have returned.
rows.anchor: this assurances was sounded to him at the time of bestowal

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says this hand sign was discussed earlier in Sūrahs al-Aʿrāf and Ṭāhā and elsewhere; he connects the qualification to the Torah’s leprosy claim, also discussed in Ṭāhā.
rows.anchor: earlier in S ūrah al-A‘r āf and S ūrah Ṭāhā

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The qualification also rejects the Torah’s claim that the whiteness of Moses’ hand resulted from leprosy.
rows.anchor: refutes the statement of the Torah as per which this whiteness of his hand was due to leprosy.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A verb like “go” is elided before the instruction about nine signs, implying that Moses should go warn Pharaoh and his people for their defiance.
rows.anchor: a verb like إذْﻫﺐ is suppressed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses initially received the staff and white hand; many further signs were concealed in them and later manifested through the staff, which supplied his full repertoire of miracles.
rows.anchor: All these signs appeared through the staff of Moses (sws). Thus in the form of the staff, he was given the complete repertoire of miracles.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nine signs here are those directed against Pharaoh and his people; signs produced for the Israelites form a distinct, numerous category also attested by the Torah.
rows.anchor: they are an entirely different category

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mubīn means “eye-opening”; prophetic miracles are unmistakable to observers and so profound that they stir even the blind.
rows.anchor: The miracles worked by prophets of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qārūn’s exemplary fate admonishes people seduced by worldly riches who forget God and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: people who were lured by the riches of this world and had forgotte n God and the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Lahab occupies Qārūn’s role in Muḥammad’s community: his wealth made a trial for himself and others, and the example is meant to open such people’s eyes.
rows.anchor: the same status as Q ārūn. He, too, was very proud of his wealth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qārūn is identified in the Torah as Korah, mentioned in Numbers chapter 19.
rows.anchor: has been mentioned in the Torah in chapter 19 of the Book of Numbers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Korah was a Levite and Moses’ and Aaron’s cousin, jealous of their political and religious leadership and arguing that others had equal right to lead.
rows.anchor: the tribe to which Moses (sws) and Aaron (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Korah challenged Moses’ and Aaron’s superiority and conspired with members of the family to rebel against Moses.
rows.anchor: rose in rebellion against Moses

rows.speaker: The Torah
rows.claim: The Torah recounts Korah son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, with Reubenites Dathan, Abiram and another associate, rising against Moses.
rows.anchor: The Torah records: Korah son of Izhar, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi

rows.speaker: The Torah
rows.claim: The Torah says 250 Israelite community leaders joined the revolt, declaring the whole community holy and questioning Moses’ and Aaron’s authority.
rows.anchor: With them were 250 Israelite men, well-k nown community leaders who had been appointed members of the council.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qārūn’s tyranny in the Qur’an refers to his rebellion against Moses.
rows.anchor: It is this rebellion of his which

words: مَآ إِنَّ مَفَاتِحَهُۥ لَتَنُوٓأُ بِٱلْعُصْبَةِ أُو۟لِى ٱلْقُوَّةِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The treasure and its keys indicate affluence, which fueled Qārūn’s rebellion and arrogance because he resented Moses’ and Aaron’s leadership.
rows.anchor: They actually point to the reason that made him rebellious and arrogant: since he was a very rich person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The keys are literal heavy latches: treasures were buried behind huge iron doors bolted with rods, requiring strong men to lift or fasten them.
rows.anchor: A group of powerful men would be needed to lift or bolt the latch.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavy keys signify wealth just as heavy food cauldrons signify generosity.
rows.anchor: Just as heavy cauldrons of food signify generosity, the existence of such keys is a sign of wealth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wise among Qārūn’s people politely warned him not to be arrogant before God, who granted his wealth and dislikes the haughty, reminding him that such people are seized by God.
rows.anchor: when Korah adopted this attitude of rebelliousness, the wise among his nation tried to persuade him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although “his people” is a general term, it refers here to the nation’s learned men; most supported Moses, while only a few with vested interests joined Qārūn.
rows.anchor: the majority of the nation was with Moses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 77 further details the learned men’s advice to Qārūn, with each sentence offering wisdom.
rows.anchor: Each and every sentence of it is a treasure of wisdom and sagacity.

words: وَٱبْتَغِ فِيمَآ ءَاتَىٰكَ ٱللَّهُ الدَّارَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth is God’s gift, not inherited property or the product of one’s own ability; it tests whether a person serves wealth or uses it to seek God’s pleasure and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: They were purely a blessing f rom God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The world is mortal; only what one spends for God’s cause benefits eternal life, while neglecting God’s and creatures’ rights and becoming enslaved to wealth leads to ruin.
rows.anchor: Only that will benefit them in their everlasting lives which today they spend for God’s cause.

rows.speaker: Our exegetes
rows.claim: The common interpretation is that one should not neglect one’s worldly share, meaning one need not abandon the world for the Hereafter; Islahi rejects this reading as incorrect.
rows.anchor: Our exegetes have generally interpreted these words to mean

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As God has been gracious to people, they should be gracious to others; God wants His attributes reflected in His creatures and dislikes miserliness.
rows.anchor: the God Who is munificent with His people does not like people who are miserly with others.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fasād is not merely theft and robbery, which are outward manifestations; its true core is arrogance, overstepping worship’s bounds and violating God’s rights and sacred limits.
rows.anchor: It does not merely connote theft and robbery

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who spread such disorder are people God dislikes, like unwanted weeds and self-invited guests in His orchard, destined to be uprooted and displaced.
rows.anchor: these weeds shall be uprooted
